title: BVA Decision 25000011: Entitlement to an effective date prior to June 16, 2014 for the grant of service connection for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is denied
text:
Citation Nr: 25000011
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 18-16 083
DATE: January 2, 2025

ORDER

Entitlement to an effective date prior to June 16, 2014 for the grant of service connection for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is denied.

FINDINGS OF FACT

1. An unappealed March 1971 rating decision denied service connection for a nervous condition, finding that the diagnosed emotionally unstable personality was a congenital abnormality not eligible for service connection.

2. In April 1971, new and material evidence, specifically, a VA medical treatment record containing diagnoses of psychoneurosis with depression and schizoid personality, was associated with the claims file; the AOJ did not issue a subsequent rating decision or otherwise address this evidence.  

3. On June 16, 2014, the AOJ received a petition to reopen a claim of entitlement to service connection for a mental health condition (posttraumatic stress disorder).

4. A September 25, 2014 VA examination report diagnosed PTSD and linked it to an in-service airplane crash.  

CONCLUSION OF LAW

The criteria for assignment of an effective date prior to June 16, 2014 for the grant of service connection for PTSD are not met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 5107, 5110; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.400.

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDINGS AND CONCLUSION

The Veteran served on active duty from July 1957 to March 1964.  This matter comes before the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) on appeal from a rating decision by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Regional Office (RO).

In February 2020, the issue on appeal was initially denied by the Board.  See BVA Decision (February 2020).  The Veteran appealed the Board's decision to the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (CAVC).  In November 2021, the CAVC issued a Memorandum Decision that affirmed the Board decision as it pertained to the issue on appeal.  See CAVC Decision at 43 (November 2021).  The Veteran argued that the Board failed to consider the effect of 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)(1) on the assigned effective date.  See CAVC Decision at 45 (November 2021).  The Veteran argued that he submitted service personnel records (SPRs) with his June 2014 claim that were not previously associated with the claims file, and that his effective date should have been granted back to January 1971, the date of his original claim for service connection.  See CAVC Decision at 45 (November 2021).  The CAVC, however, affirmed the Board decision, finding that the Veteran did not support these claims with sufficient argument or evidence.  See CAVC Decision at 47 (November 2021)

The Veteran appealed the CAVC Memorandum Decision to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.  See Thomas v. McDonough, 97 F.4th 850 (March 2024).  The Federal Circuit vacated the CAVC decision and remanded for further action, noting that the Board did not consider 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)(1) in its decision.  See Thomas, 97 F.4th at 854.  In a September 2024 Memorandum Decision, the CAVC effectuated the Federal Circuit's decision and remanded the issue to the Board for consideration of 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c).  See CAVC Decision (September 2024). 

A September 2024 Board letter notified the Veteran he had 90 days to submit any additional evidence or argument.  See BVA Post CAVC Notice (September 2024).  In October 2024, the Veteran's attorney submitted argument in support of the appeal.  See Appellate Brief (October 2024).  The Veteran submitted SPRs that were mostly duplicative of those already of record or irrelevant.  See STR - Medical (October 2024).  As the substantive appeal was submitted after February 2, 2013, remand is not required for AOJ consideration.  See 38 U.S.C. § 7105(e) (2014).  Accordingly, the Board may proceed to adjudicate the issue on appeal.

Effective Dates

Generally, the effective date of an award of disability compensation based on an original claim shall be the date of receipt of the claim or the date entitlement arose, whichever is later.  38 U.S.C. § 5110(a); 38 C.F.R. § 3.400.  Unless otherwise provided, the effective date of compensation will be fixed in accordance with the facts found, but will not be earlier than the date of receipt of the claimant's application.  38 U.S.C. § 5110(a).  If a claim is filed within one year after separation from service, service connection will be effective as of the day after separation.  38 C.F.R. § 3.400(b)(2).  

Prior to March 24, 2015, a claim was "a formal or informal communication in writing requesting a determination of entitlement, or evidencing a belief in entitlement, to a benefit."  38 C.F.R. § 3.1(p).  An informal claim is "[a]ny communication or action indicating intent to apply for one or more benefits."  38 C.F.R. § 3.155(a).  VA must look to all communications from a claimant that may be interpreted as applications or claims - formal and informal - for benefits and is required to identify and act on informal claims for benefits.  Servello v. Derwinski, 3 Vet. App. 196, 198 (1992).  The essential elements for any claim, whether formal or informal, are: (1) an intent to apply for benefits; (2) an identification of the benefits sought; and (3) a communication in writing.  Brokowski v. Shinseki, 23 Vet. App. 79, 84 (2009); MacPhee v. Nicholson, 459 F.3d 1323, 1326-27 (Fed. Cir. 2006) (holding that the plain language of the regulations requires a claimant to have intent to file a claim for VA benefits).

With regard to the date of entitlement, the term date entitlement arose is the date when the claimant met the requirements for the benefits sought, on a facts found basis.  38 U.S.C. § 5110(a); McGrath v. Gober, 14 Vet. App. 28, 35 (2000).  These facts found include the date the disability first manifested and the date entitlement to benefits was authorized by law and regulation.  See generally 38 C.F.R. § 3.400.  For instance, if a claimant filed a claim for benefits for a disability before he actually had the disability, the effective date for benefits can be no earlier than the date the disability first manifested.  Ellington v. Peake, 541 F.3d 1364, 1369-70 (Fed. Cir. 2008).  However, the date entitlement arose is not the date that the RO receives the evidence, but the date to which that evidence refers.  McGrath, 14 Vet. App. at 35.  "[I]t is the information in a medical opinion, and not the date the medical opinion was provided that is relevant when assigning an effective date."  Tatum v. Shinseki, 24 Vet. App. 139, 145 (2010).

Further, new and material evidence received prior to the expiration of the appeal period will be considered as having been filed in connection with the claim which was pending at the beginning of the appeal period.  38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b).  When VA receives evidence prior to the expiration of the appeal period, the claim remains pending until VA makes a determination that is directly responsive as to whether this evidence constitutes new and material evidence.  Turner v. Shulkin, 29 Vet. App. 207, 211 (2018); Beraud v. McDonald, 766 F.3d 1402, 1407 (Fed. Cir. 2014).  

New evidence is defined as existing evidence not previously submitted to agency decision makers.  Material evidence means evidence that, by itself or when considered with previous evidence of record, relates to an unestablished fact necessary to substantiate the claim.  New and material evidence can be neither cumulative nor redundant of the evidence previously of record and must raise a reasonable possibility of substantiating the claim.  38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b).    

Finally, at any time after VA issues a decision on a claim, if VA receives or associates with the claims file relevant official service department records that existed but were not associated with the claims file when VA first decided the claim, VA will reconsider the claim, rather than requiring new and material evidence.  38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)(1).  An award made based all or in part on the records identified by paragraph(c)(1) of this section is effective on the date entitlement arose or the date VA received the previously decided claim, whichever is later, or such other date as may be authorized by the provisions of this part applicable to the previously decided claim.  38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)(3).  A retroactive evaluation of disability resulting from disease or injury subsequently service connected on the basis of the new evidence from the service department must be supported adequately by medical evidence.  38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)(4).  

A precedential decision issued by the Federal Circuit Court, Lang v. Wilkie, 971 F.3d 1348 (Fed. Cir. 2020), addressed the application of the constructive possession rule of Bell v. Derwinski, 2 Vet. App. 611, 613 (1992) (holding that documents within VA's control are generally considered to be part of the record), to 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b), which provides that new and material evidence received within the one-year appeal period is considered as having been filed in connection with the pending claim. The Federal Circuit Court overruled the Court's decision in Turner v. Shulkin, 29 Vet. App. 207 (2018), in which the Court held that the constructive possession rule applies to 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b), but with the limitation that VA adjudicators must have had sufficient knowledge that such documents existed at the time. The Federal Circuit Court held that this additional requirement is contrary to law and the regular constructive possession principle applies to 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b) without this limitation. Specifically, "evidence is constructively received by the VA adjudicator post-decision if it (1) was generated by the VA or was submitted to the VA and (2) can reasonably be expected to be connected to the veteran's claim."

Entitlement to an effective date prior to June 16, 2014 for the grant of service connection for PTSD.

The Veteran's attorney argues that an earlier effective date is warranted for the award of service connection for PTSD.  See Appellate Brief (October 2024).  The attorney asserts that VA initially denied the Veteran's claim in 1971 for service connection based on a finding that the diagnosis was a personality disorder that is not a disability for VA purposes, based in part on service treatment records, and that the claim had been reopened and granted, in part, based on service personnel records the Veteran had been submitted.  See Appellate Brief at 1-2 (October 2024).  The attorney contends that the claim for service connection should have been reconsidered, rather than reopened, and that an effective date in January 1971 is appropriate.  See Appellate Brief at 2 (October 2024).  

The Board concludes that the criteria for assignment of an effective date prior to June 16, 2014 for the grant of service connection for PTSD are not met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 5107, 5110; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.400.

The procedural history and factual background are relevant here.  The record reflects that the Veteran served on active duty from July 1957 to March 1964.  See Certificate of Release or Discharge From Active Duty (June 2014); Certificate of Release or Discharge From Active Duty (August 2014).  In January 1971, VA received the Veteran's VA 21-526 claim for entitlement to service connection for depressive mania, which he asserted began in 1961 after an aircraft accident in which several of his fellow service-members were killed.  See VA 21-526 Veterans Application for Compensation or Pension (January 1971).  The AOJ obtained service treatment records (STRs).  See STR - Medical (March 1971).  

The STRs show that on March 10, 1964, the Veteran was picked up by shore patrol at the request of his wife who was afraid he was going to commit suicide.  He had been previously hospitalized at the US Naval Hospital in Newport, Rhode Island.  See STR - Medical at 10 (March 1971).  The diagnosis was emotionally unstable personality, passive aggressive, moderately severe.  See STR - Medical at 10 (March 1971).  He was referred to the US Naval Hospital in Memphis, Tennessee for admission, evaluation, and treatment.  See STR - Medical at 10 (March 1971).  The initial diagnosis was passive-aggressive personality, did not exist prior to service entrance.  See STR - Medical at 12 (March 1971).  He reported mainly stressors related to his marriage.  See STR - Medical at 12 (March 1971).  Upon further evaluation, the clinician noted family stressors and diagnosed psychoneurosis, mixed, did not exist prior to service entrance.  See STR - Medical at 14 (March 1971).  Five days following admission, he was granted special liberty and at that time he took unauthorized absence; he then turned himself in at the San Diego Naval Hospital.  See STR - Medical at 14 (March 1971).  

At the San Diego Naval Hospital, the Veteran reported that his difficulties began in 1961 when he was involved in an airplane accident in which several crew members were killed, but he was able to get himself out.  See STR - Medical at 4 (March 1971).  Since that time, he reported difficulty with drinking, intermittent depression, and family trouble.  He reported that he cut his wrists and was on the psychiatric service and was then sent to the Naval Air Station in Memphis.  He was angry about this, so he left, but then decided to turn himself in.  See STR - Medical at 4 (March 1971).  The diagnosis was revised from depressive reaction, not due to his misconduct and in the line of duty, to neurotic depressive reaction.  See STR - Medical at 4-5 (March 1971).  

The Veteran was then admitted to the US Naval Hospital in Oakland, California on April 4, 1964.  See STR - Medical at 8, 69 (March 1971).  A Report of Board Medical Survey case history noted that the Veteran revealed evidence of life-long adjustive techniques which satisfactorily served the Veteran under favorable conditions, but failed when he came under stress.  See STR-Medical at 71 (March 1971).  It was noted that the Veteran joined the Navy in 1957 and did well in his assignments and performance.  In 1960, he began to experience marital stresses that resulted in irritability, jealousy, and hostility.  He re-enlisted in 1962, and immediately following, in succession, were an airplane crash, a Captain's mast, increased marital conflict, excessive alcoholic intake, and intermittent depression.  See STR - Medical at 71 (March 1971).  The Veteran stated that the depression reached the point where he cut his wrists in Rhode Island, and was hospitalized from October to December 1963, was released and was then sent to the US Naval Air Station in Memphis where he began to drink to excess, became depressed, and then his wife had him hospitalized.  He was very angry about this and decided to leave, but then later turned himself in.  See STR - Medical at 71 (March 1971).  The examiner noted that after an adequate period of observation, treatment, a conference of staff psychiatrists, and review of available records and current findings, it was agreed that the Veteran had shown long standing evidence of pathological emotional immaturity.  See STR - Medical at 71 (March 1971).  On April 20, 1964, the diagnosis was revised to emotional unstable personality, manifested by irritability, dependency, depression, impulsive behavior, anxiety, difficulties with social and work relationships, impaired judgment, and impulsive behavior under relatively minor stress.  The clinicians noted moderate predisposition with a history of neuropathic traits in childhood with persistence of adolescent defense mechanisms.  See STR - Medical at 71-72 (March 1971).  The Report of Board Medical Survey noted that the Veteran suffered from an immature personality which renders him unsuitable for further service in the Navy and that he "suffers from no disability which is the result of an incident of service, or which was aggravated thereby."  See STR - Medical at 72 (March 1971).  Discharge was recommended as the Veteran was unsuitable for service.  See STR - Medical at 70 (March 1971).  

A March 1971 rating decision AOJ denied service connection for a nervous condition, noting that there was a careful and complete psychiatric evaluation in the March and April 1964 STRs with a final diagnosis of emotionally unstable personality.  See Rating Decision (March 1971).  Without any significant discussion, the AOJ noted that an emotionally unstable personality was a constitutional or development abnormality which was not a disability under the law.  See Rating Decision (March 1971).  The AOJ did not address whether the in-service accident occurred, appearing to accept the extensive histories contained in the STRs.  

In April 1971, a VA treatment record was associated with the claims file that noted a diagnosis of psychoneurosis with depression, moderate, and schizoid personality.  See Medical Treatment Record - Non-Government Facility (April 1971).  The Veteran was hospitalized from December 1970 to February 1971.  See Medical Treatment Record - Non-Government Facility (April 1971).

The next submission from the Veteran was on June 16, 2014; on this date, VA received the Veteran's petition to reopen the previously denied claim for service connection for a mental health condition.  See VA 21-526EZ, Fully Developed Claim (June 2014).  As part of that claim, the Veteran submitted SPRs.  See Military Personnel Record (June 2014).  Those records included performance reviews showing high scores, to include at basic training.  See Military Personnel Record at 1, 3, 5-6 (June 2014).  The Veteran also submitted lay statements regarding the in-service airplane accident and his changed behavior after military service.  See Buddy/Lay Statement (August 2014); Buddy/Lay Statement (May 2014).  The Veteran also submitted a newspaper article that showed the survivors of the airplane accident, including the Veteran.  See Correspondence (September 2014).  

A September 25, 2014 VA examination was obtained; the VA clinician noted that due to connectivity issues, the claims file was not available to review and that they only reviewed VA treatment records.  See C&P Exam at 2 (October 2014).  The examination report contained a lengthy medical history review elicited from the Veteran.  See C&P Exam at 2 (October 2014).  The clinician noted the Veteran's in-service stressor of an airplane crash in 1961 and that the Veteran met all the criteria for a diagnosis of PTSD.  See C&P Exam at 4-5 (October 2014).  The clinician also noted that the Veteran's history of his stressor and the pattern of symptoms over time were consistent with a diagnosis of PTSD and his current presentation also warranted this diagnosis.  See C&P Exam at 5 (October 2014).  Thus, the clinician opined that that the PTSD was at least as likely as not related to the Veteran's military stressor.  See C&P Exam at 8 (October 2014).

Next, a November 2014 rating decision granted service connection for PTSD, noting that it had been established as directly related to military service; no further explanation was provided.  See Rating Decision (November 2014).  The AOJ assigned a 30 percent evaluation, effective June 16, 2014, the date of VA's receipt of the Veteran's claim to reopen.  This appeal arises from the Veteran's disagreement with the assigned effective date for the award of service connection for PTSD.

Having carefully reviewed the record and contentions, the Board finds that the weight of the evidence is against the claim for an earlier effective date even accepting that the date of claim is January 20, 1971, as explained below.

First, the Board finds that the date of claim is January 20, 1971, the date the AOJ received the Veteran's initial claim for service connection for depressive mania.  See VA 21-526 Veterans Application for Compensation or Pension (January 1971).  As noted above, the AOJ obtained the Veteran's STRs at that time; thereafter, it denied the claim for service connection based on the finding that those records showed the Veteran's psychiatric condition was a congenital abnormality, which is not a disability for VA purposes.  See STR - Medical (March 1971); Rating Decision (March 1971).  The Veteran was notified of this decision in April 1971.  See Notification Letter (April 1971).  

Then, on April 19, 1971, a VA treatment record was associated with the claims file.  The record shows hospitalization for mental health treatment from December 7, 1970 to February 11, 1971 at a VA Hospital in Phoenix, Arizona.  See Medical Treatment Record - Government Facility (April 1971).  The Veteran was transferred from a private hospital for chronic depression, and he reported prior treatment for depression in various Naval Hospitals before separation from service in 1964.  The record noted diagnoses of moderate psychoneurosis with depression and schizoid personality.  See Medical Treatment Record - Government Facility (April 1971).  Because this medical record potentially contains a diagnosis of a psychiatric disorder that is not a congenital disorder, depression, it is new and material evidence that was not previously before the AOJ.  See 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b).  Additionally, the AOJ did not make a determination that was directly responsive as to whether this record constitutes new and material evidence, via a rating decision or other mechanism.  See Beraud v. McDonald, 766 F.3d 1402, 1406-07 (Fed. Cir. 2014) (holding that a claim remains pending where VA failed to fulfill a statutory duty to determine the character of newly submitted evidence and declining to presume that VA considered records of which it had notice, but never obtained); Bond v. Shinseki, 659 F.3d 1362 (Fed. Cir. 2011) (noting that 3.156(b) requires VA to determine whether subsequently submitted evidence constituted new and material evidence relating to an earlier claim); 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(a)-(b). See also, Turner, 29 Vet. App. at 211.  Thus, the January 1971 claim remained pending.  See 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b).  

Second, the Board finds that the date of entitlement is September 25, 2014, the date of the VA examination that diagnosed PTSD and provided a positive nexus opinion linking PTSD to the in-service airplane crash incident.  See C&P Exam (October 2014).  As noted in the January 1971 rating decision, the STRs showed evidence of significant psychiatric symptoms during service, but after extensive treatment and discussion, the military clinicians determined the proper diagnosis was an immature personality disorder.  See STR - Medical at 72 (March 1971).  The AOJ relied on this finding when determining that the Veteran's psychiatric disability was congenital and developmental and not eligible for service connection.  See Rating Decision (May 1971); 38 C.F.R. § 3.303(c).  VA treatment records dated in 1971 show several psychiatric diagnoses, including depression.  See Medical Treatment Record - Government Facility (April 1971).  Other VA treatment records associated with the claims file from 1971 to 2014 noted possible PTSD and PTSD symptoms.  See CAPRI at 19, 46, 54, 57, 61 (September 2014).  But no VA or private treatment records provided a nexus opinion linking the Veteran's psychiatric disorder to the in-service incident until the October 2014 VA examination and opinion.  See C&P Exam (October 2014).  Such a nexus is required by law and regulations prior to a grant of service connection.  See 38 C.F.R. § 3.303(a), (f).  Notably, prior to this VA etiological opinion, the evidence was not clear whether there was a psychiatric disorder eligible for service connection.  See STR - Medical (March 1971); see also CAPRI at 19, 46, 54, 57, 61 (September 2014).  Thus, these records do not support an earlier date of entitlement.

The Board acknowledges that there appears to have been psychiatric symptoms since service and that this too, can be a basis for service connection.  See 38 C.F.R. § 3.303(b).  But the in-service military clinicians determined the psychiatric complaints were part of a congenital abnormality, rather than a chronic disease.  See STR - Medical at 72 (March 1971).  Additionally, the 1971 VA medical records indicated several diagnoses, including depression, but did not link this psychiatric disorder to service or otherwise indicate that the prior diagnosis of a personality disorder was erroneous.  See e.g., Medical Treatment Record - Government Facility (April 1971).  Thus, the evidence of record does not support a grant of service connection for a psychiatric disability as a chronic disease with continuity of symptomatology.

Given the above, the Board finds that the later of the date of claim (January 20, 1970) and date of entitlement (September 25, 2014) is, therefore, September 25, 2014.  Hence, the Board finds no basis upon which to assign an effective date prior to June 16, 2014.

Moreover, the Board notes that it has not expressly addressed the Veteran's and his attorney's argument that the claim should have been reconsidered rather than reopened as he submitted service personnel records with his 2014 petition to reopen.  See Appellate Brief at 3-4 (October 2014); see also 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c).  The Board's decision herein regarding the date of claim places the date of claim at the earliest date possible - the first claim the Veteran made in 1971.  Thus, the Board need not address these arguments as no earlier date of claim is available.  

Furthermore, the Board notes that the June 2014 VA clinician did not review the claims file, including the newly submitted SPRs; thus, the opinion linking the current PTSD to the incident during service did not rely on those documents.  See C&P Exam at 2 (October 2014).  Thus, the award of service connection was not made based on all or in part on these records.  See 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)(3).  Moreover, although the Veteran went to great lengths to substantiate the existence of the in-service airplane crash incident, the occurrence of this incident was never disputed by the AOJ.  See Correspondence (October 2014); Buddy/Lay Statement (October 2014); Correspondence (September 2014); Buddy/Lay Statement (August 2014); Correspondence (June 2014); Buddy/Lay Statement (May 2014).  Rather, as noted by the AOJ in a 2014 examination request, the evidence contained in the STRs obtained in 1971 substantiate the in-service event.  See CAPRI (September 2014).

Finally, the Board has considered the Veteran's attorney's assertions that an earlier effective date should be granted because the STRs were inconsistent by providing that a personality disorder did not exist prior to service entrance, and by changing the psychiatric diagnoses during the Veteran's active service.  See Appellate Brief at 3 (October 2024).  The Veteran's attorney thus appears to argue there was clear and unmistakable error (CUE) in the denial of service connection in the March 1971 rating decision.  See Appellate Brief at 3 (October 2024).  As determined above, however, the March 1971 rating decision was not final and the January 1971 claim remained pending.  Thus, the rating decision was not final and may not be the subject of a motion for reversal or revision based on CUE.  See 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(a); Smith v. Brown, 35 F.3d 1516, 1527 (Fed. Cir. 1994).  

A retroactive evaluation of disability resulting from disease or injury subsequently service connected on the basis of the new evidence from the service department must be supported adequately by medical evidence.  38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)(4).  As noted above, service connection was not supported adequately by medical evidence prior to the September 2014 VA examination.  At that time, the STRs showed an in-service incident and evidence of significant psychiatric symptoms during service, but after extensive treatment and discussion, the military clinicians determined the proper diagnosis was an immature personality disorder.  See STR - Medical at 72 (March 1971).  1971 VA treatment records dated show several psychiatric diagnoses, including psychoneurosis, depression, and schizoid personality.  This record did not mention or address the in-service airplane crash and did not link the diagnoses to any incident or injury.  See Medical Treatment Record - Government Facility (April 1971).  

Other VA treatment records associated with the claims file dated from 1971 to 2014 noted possible PTSD and PTSD symptoms.  See CAPRI at 19, 46, 54, 57, 61 (September 2014).  But no VA or private treatment records provided a nexus opinion linking the Veteran's psychiatric disorder to the in-service incident until the October 2014 VA examination and opinion.  The records also did not otherwise indicate that the prior diagnosis of a personality disorder was erroneous.  Thus, the evidence does not show a psychiatric disorder due to service that is supported adequately by medical evidence.  38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)(4).  

Accordingly, the claim is denied. As the evidence of record persuasively weighs against the claim, the benefit-of-the-doubt rule does not apply.  38 U.S.C. § 5107(b); 38 C.F.R. § 3.102; Lynch v. McDonough, 21 F.4th 776 (2021).

 

 

C.A. SKOW

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	K.M., Counsel

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided. This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.
